newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: SMITHKLINE SAYS IMPRESSED WITH HYCAMTIN DRUG.
newsitem.headline: SMITHKLINE SAYS IMPRESSED WITH HYCAMTIN DRUG.

text.p: DUBLIN, Aug 14 - British-based pharmaceuticals group SmithKline Beecham Plc said on Thursday its new cancer drug Hycamtin had shown "impressive" results in fighting small cell lung cancer when used in combination with Bristol Myers Squibb Co's drug Taxol.

In a presentation at the eighth world conference on lung cancer, scientists said a small Phase II trial of the therapy at the University of Pittsburgh indicated the combination was at least as good as existing combinations of drugs used in first-stage treatment of the disease.

Dr James Jett of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, lead investigator in the trial, said "given the low survival rates of patients with small cell lung cancer, there is a compelling need for new therapies to treat this type of cancer."

He said 12 out of 14 patients in the trial responded to the drugs, with four seeing a complete disappearance of signs and symptoms of the disease and eight experiencing a partial response, with tumours shrinking by at least 50 percent.

Small cell is the most aggressive form of lung cancer, and accounts for between 20 and 25 percent of lung cancer cases. Most sufferers are smokers or former smokers, and the disease is often only diagnosed when it is at an advanced stage.
With current treatment, patients whose disease is already well advanced survive for an average of nine months after diagnosis, and less than ten percent are still alive after two years.
Jett said 51 percent of patients treated in the Pittsburgh trial were still alive after one year, falling to 26 percent after 18 months, the most up-to-date figure available.

Hycamtin is already approved for treatment of ovarian cancer in the U.S. and European Union, and is being investigated for a wide range of other cancers, including breast, colorectal, pancreatic, prostate and cervical.
The drug acts by inhibiting an enzyme, topoisomerase, which is crucial for the replication of DNA in human cells.
Taxol, which is derived from yew trees, is approved in Europe and the U.S. as a treatment for ovarian cancer and was recently approved for use in the AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma.
